items.answer: Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.

Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

The systemic definition of augmented reality (AR) states that an AR system should have three characteristics: combining the real world with virtual content, being interactive in real time so that interaction with the digital content added to the real-world view is reflected immediately, and being registered in 3D.

Field of view (FOV) is a content-related factor in virtual reality (VR) that affects susceptibility to cybersickness (CS), and it is the extent to which the display in a VR headset captures the user's field of vision.
Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).

data.text: Augmented reality devices are categorized into headsets and glasses, handheld devices, projection-based systems, spatial augmented reality, head-up displays, and AR contact lenses. Examples include the Microsoft HoloLens, Google Glass, smartphones, and interactive projectors. Head-up displays are typically found in cars, while AR contact lenses are the latest technology being explored. These categories serve various application domains, such as education, retail, industrial design, healthcare, and medical development.
points: Augmented reality devices are categorized into headsets and glasses, handheld devices, projection-based systems, spatial augmented reality, head-up displays, and AR contact lenses.
Examples include the Microsoft HoloLens, Google Glass, Vuzix Blade Glasses, smartphones, tablets, and Nintendo devices.
Projection-based systems and spatial augmented reality include interactive projectors, AR sandboxes, projection mapping software, laser projectors, and projection keyboards.
Head-up displays are typically found in cars, while AR contact lenses are the latest technology being explored.
These AR categories serve various application domains, including education, retail, industrial design, healthcare, and medical development.

questions.question: Compared with VR headsets, what general characteristic is stated for AR headsets?
options: They are smaller and more immersive and provide a wider field of view.
They are smaller, less immersive, and provide a narrower field of view.
They are larger and more immersive but provide a narrower field of view.
They are larger, more immersive, and provide a wider field of view.
questions.explanation: AR headsets are described as larger and more immersive, presenting real-world and augmented digital content with a wider field of view.

questions.question: What built-in sensors are typically included in AR headsets?
options: Built-in speakers and projectors.
Only microphones and speakers.
External cameras and depth sensors.
Cameras and depth sensors.
questions.explanation: AR headsets typically include built-in sensors, often cameras and depth sensors.

questions.question: Why do VR headsets typically have fewer components than an AR headset such as Microsoft HoloLens?
options: Because VR does not need to provide a virtual view.
Because AR headsets use smaller displays than VR headsets.
Because VR does not need to provide a real-world view.
Because AR headsets use fewer cameras than VR headsets.
questions.explanation: VR headsets usually have fewer components than an AR headset such as Microsoft HoloLens because VR does not need to provide a real-world view.

questions.question: In Microsoft HoloLens, how does interaction with the device take place?
options: Through a keyboard, mouse, and handheld controller.
Through eye movements, voice commands, and hand motions.
Through only voice commands and eye movements.
Through touch gestures on a visible screen.
questions.explanation: Interaction in the Microsoft HoloLens takes place through eye movements, voice commands, and hand motions, with the device detecting these inputs.

questions.question: What does Microsoft HoloLens integrate with the real-world view obtained through its special glasses?
options: Only audio recordings and music.
A fully virtual environment with no real-world view.
High-definition holograms or digital content.
Simpler heads-up display-type overlays.
questions.explanation: Microsoft HoloLens integrates high-definition holograms or digital content with the real-world view obtained through its special glasses.

data.text: AR headsets are generally larger and more immersive than VR headsets, providing a wider field of view and blending real-world content with digital content. These headsets typically include built-in sensors like cameras and depth sensors, whereas VR headsets often have fewer components because they do not need to provide a real-world view. Additionally, AR headsets can integrate digital content with a real-world view and support interactions through eye movements, voice commands, and hand motions.
points: AR headsets are generally larger and more immersive, providing a wider field of view and blending real-world content with digital content.
AR headsets typically include built-in sensors, such as cameras and depth sensors.
VR headsets typically have fewer components than AR headsets because they do not need to provide a real-world view.
AR headsets can integrate digital content with a real-world view and support interactions through eye movements, voice commands, and hand motions.

questions.question: Which statement best describes how AR smart glasses differ from AR headsets?
options: AR smart glasses provide full 3D holograms, while AR headsets provide only simpler heads-up display overlays.
AR headsets have a smaller field of view and are less powerful than AR smart glasses.
AR headsets are lighter, less immersive, and more comfortable for extended wear than AR smart glasses.
AR smart glasses are lighter, less immersive, and more comfortable for extended wear than AR headsets.
questions.explanation: AR smart glasses are lighter, less immersive, usually have a smaller field of view, are less powerful, and are more comfortable to wear for extended periods, whereas AR headsets are more powerful wearables.

questions.question: Why do AR headsets provide full 3D holograms instead of the simpler heads-up display overlays found in AR smart glasses?
options: They rely primarily on marker-based tracking of printed symbols.
They use handheld cameras to capture live real-world views and overlay content on a screen.
They project graphical information directly onto physical objects in the room.
They contain more components, sensors, and projectors than AR smart glasses.
questions.explanation: AR headsets can present full 3D holograms because they contain more components, sensors, and projectors than AR smart glasses.

questions.question: How do handheld AR devices typically present augmented content to the user?
options: They replace the real-world view with a fully virtual scene on the device screen.
They display digital content on physical surfaces in the real world using projectors.
They provide a heads-up display through lightweight glasses with a smaller field of view.
They show a live camera view on the device screen and overlay digital content on top of it.
questions.explanation: Handheld AR devices use their own camera to capture a live real-world image that is displayed on the device screen, then overlay digital content on top of that live real-world view.

questions.question: What two types of AR technology do handheld AR devices typically rely on?
options: Marker-based AR and markerless AR.
Spatial augmented AR and tabletop AR.
Head-tracked AR and eye-tracked AR.
Marker-based AR and full 3D holographic AR.
questions.explanation: Handheld AR devices typically rely on marker-based AR and markerless AR.

data.text: AR smart glasses are lighter and more comfortable than AR headsets but provide simpler heads-up display overlays instead of 3D holograms. Examples of these devices include Google Glass, Vuzix's Blade, Epson glasses, and Magic Leap glasses. Handheld AR devices like smartphones and tablets are the most common and accessible options, using cameras to overlay digital content on real-world images via marker-based or markerless technologies.
points: AR smart glasses are lighter and more comfortable than AR headsets but are less immersive and less powerful.
Smart glasses provide simpler heads-up display overlays whereas headsets provide full 3D holograms.
Examples of smart glasses include Google Glass, Vuzix's Blade, Epson glasses, and Magic Leap glasses.
Handheld AR devices like smartphones and tablets are the most common and accessible AR devices.
Handheld AR devices use a camera to capture real-world images and overlay digital content using marker-based or markerless technologies.

questions.question: Compared with AR headsets, glasses, or handheld devices, where does a spatial AR system place its digital content?
options: On a transparent visor in front of the user's eyes.
In a fully virtual environment with no real objects visible.
On the screen of a device held by the user.
On physical objects in the real world rather than on the user's view.
questions.explanation: Spatial AR projects digital content onto physical objects, while headsets, glasses, and handheld devices place it in the user's own view or on a device screen.

questions.question: What interaction advantage does spatial AR have over AR headsets, glasses, or handheld devices?
options: Each user can see only private content on a personal display.
Only one user can interact with the system at a time.
Multiple users can interact simultaneously with the same augmented content.
Interaction requires every user to hold a separate device.
questions.explanation: Spatial AR augments a shared physical object, allowing several users to interact with the same content at the same time.

questions.question: What is the fundamental principle of a spatial AR system?
options: It projects images onto a transparent surface worn by the user.
It adds virtual objects to the physical environment so they appear to coexist in the same space.
It replaces the physical environment with a completely virtual scene.
It overlays digital content only on a camera view shown on a screen.
questions.explanation: A spatial AR system augments the physical environment by making virtual objects seem to coexist with real objects.

questions.question: How does an air sandbox update its projected topographic map?
options: It relies on the users wearing AR glasses to see the updated map.
It uses a static precomputed image that does not change while users move the sand.
It captures a live view on a smartphone screen and overlays the map there.
A sensor, such as a 3D camera, detects changes in the sand or gestures in real time.
questions.explanation: An air sandbox uses a projector and a sensor to project and update the map as users move sand or gesture.

questions.question: What does projection mapping do in a spatial AR context?
options: It displays a map on a physical box of sand and updates it as the sand moves.
It creates complex projections onto three-dimensional space without a physical surface.
It projects a virtual keyboard onto a flat tabletop for typing.
It overlays digital content on the live camera view of a handheld device.
questions.explanation: Projection mapping is a software-based spatial AR application that uses standard projectors to make complex 3D projections, such as an Earth model in air.

data.text: Spatial augmented reality (AR) devices use projectors to overlay virtual content onto the physical environment. These systems are not tied to the user and allow multiple people to interact with the content simultaneously. Implementing these systems requires understanding the geometry and lighting of the environment, which is why they are used in various domains like education, art, and entertainment.
points: Spatial augmented reality (AR) devices use projectors to overlay virtual content onto the physical environment.
These devices are not tied to the user and allow multiple people to interact with the content simultaneously.
Implementing these systems requires understanding the geometry and lighting of the environment using sensors or computer vision.
Categories of spatial AR include interactive projectors, air sandboxes, projection keyboards, and projection mapping.
Spatial AR systems are used in various fields such as education, medical training, and entertainment.

questions.question: Which statement describes a head-up display in AR hardware?
options: It projects images onto a transparent surface such as a screen or visor.
It replaces the user's view of the real world with a fully virtual environment.
It places digital content directly on a lens on the wearer's eye.
It overlays digital content on physical objects in the surrounding environment.
questions.explanation: A head-up display is an AR display category that projects images onto a transparent surface, ideally making only the content visible.

questions.question: Which AR display category is commonly used in cars and aircraft?
options: A spatial augmented reality system
A handheld AR device
An AR contact lens
A head-up display
questions.explanation: Head-up displays are commonly used in cars and aircraft.

questions.question: What makes AR contact lenses an emerging future wearable display?
options: They project images onto a transparent visor.
They are very small, can be placed directly on the eye, and are not visible to outsiders.
They are bulky and require elaborate setups.
They are difficult to hold for a long time.
questions.explanation: AR contact lenses are an emerging future wearable because they are very small, can be placed directly on the eye, and are not visible to outsiders.

questions.question: How do AR contact lenses present information to the wearer?
options: By displaying a fully virtual environment around the user
By projecting interfaces onto any surface
By superimposing digital images or information directly on the lens.
By overlaying content on physical objects in a room
questions.explanation: AR contact lenses superimpose digital images or information onto the wearer's field of vision directly on the lens.

questions.question: What open issue is associated with AR contact lenses?
options: They are too bulky to be used as a wearable display.
They require a transparent visor with visible borders.
They are difficult to hold for long periods.
Their effect on users is not well known, and changing information in front of the eyes may affect behavior or cause sickness.
questions.explanation: The effect of AR contact lenses is not well known or researched, and seeing a lot of changing information directly in front of the eyes may affect normal behavior or cause sickness.

data.text: Head-up displays project images onto transparent surfaces and are commonly used in cars and aircraft. While current AR hardware is often bulky or difficult to hold, AR contact lenses are an emerging technology that superimposes information directly onto a wearer's field of vision. These lenses can contain miniaturized components, but their effects on the user are not well known or researched.
points: Head-up displays project images onto transparent surfaces and are commonly used in cars and aircraft.
Many current AR hardware systems are bulky, require elaborate setups, or can be difficult to hold for long periods.
AR contact lenses are a future wearable technology that superimposes digital information directly onto a wearer's field of vision.
These lenses can contain miniaturized components, but their effects on the user are not well known or researched.

questions.question: Why is field of view both a design advantage of AR headsets over AR smart glasses and a display factor that was linked to cybersickness in VR?
questions.reference_answer: AR headsets are larger and more immersive, present more content in the form of real-world content and augmented digital content, and provide a wider field of view. AR smart glasses are lighter, less immersive, less powerful, and usually have a smaller field of view, making them more comfortable to wear for extended periods. Field of view was described as a content-related factor affecting susceptibility to cybersickness in VR, so the size of the displayed view matters for both immersion and comfort.

questions.question: How does the need to present a real-world view shape the component differences between an AR headset such as the Microsoft HoloLens and a VR headset?
questions.reference_answer: An AR system is expected to combine the real world with virtual content, interact in real time, and register in 3D, so an AR headset may include cameras and depth sensors to obtain a real-world view. A VR headset does not need to provide a real-world view, so it may omit some advanced AR features and typically has fewer components than an AR headset. For example, the Microsoft HoloLens integrates high-definition holograms with the real-world view obtained through its special glasses.

questions.question: Why can spatial augmented reality support simultaneous multi-user interaction more directly than AR headsets, smart glasses, and handheld AR devices?
questions.reference_answer: Spatial augmented reality systems overlay digital content directly on physical objects in the real world rather than on the user's own view. Their display element is not tied to or held by a single user, which can make the interface more natural and intuitive. This shared augmented physical content allows multiple users to interact simultaneously, unlike headsets, glasses, or handheld devices where each user interacts only with content on that user's own device.

questions.question: Why are AR contact lenses considered a future wearable display that can be placed directly on the eye without being visible to outsiders, and what unresolved user-effect issue remains with them?
questions.reference_answer: AR contact lenses are very small, can be placed directly on the eye like a regular contact lens, and are not visible to outsiders, making them an emerging future wearable display technology. They superimpose digital images or information directly onto the wearer's field of vision. Their effect on the user is not well known or researched, and seeing a lot of changing information directly in front of the eyes may affect normal behavior or cause some sort of sickness.
